title: Abortion
scope: When a developing human acquires moral status, against bodily autonomy, and what the law should permit.

overview.summary: What an embryo or fetus is owed, what a pregnant woman is owed, and what the law should do when the two claims collide.
overview.scope_covered: When a developing human acquires moral status; whether a woman’s claim over her own body settles the question anyway; the embryology and neuroscience both sides cite; what permissive and restrictive regimes produce; public opinion; and the legal arrangements societies have reached.
overview.scope_excluded: Contraception, in vitro fertilization and embryo selection, except where a position on abortion forces a position on them; what is owed to animals or artificial minds; and the electoral horse race. Abortion numbers appear here to show what rides on the question, not to argue that any number is too high or too low.
overview.why_now: Four US states put abortion measures on the November 3, 2026 ballot. Missouri’s Amendment 3 would repeal the reproductive-rights amendment Missourians approved in 2024 and replace it with a ban carrying narrow exceptions; the measures in Idaho, Nevada and Virginia would protect access.

stats.label: Americans holding each framing of the question
stats.note: 52 percent of US adults say the view that the decision belongs solely to the pregnant woman describes them extremely or very well, and 39 percent say that of an embryo being a person with rights.
stats.detail: Pew put the two claims to the same people as separate statements rather than forcing a choice, and the shares overlap: about a third of adults say both describe their views at least somewhat well. For the first statement, 20 percent say it fits somewhat well and 27 percent not too or not at all well; for the second, 17 percent somewhat and 43 percent not too or not at all. The same survey put support for legal abortion in all or most cases at 60 percent against 38 percent for illegal in all or most, down from 63 percent legal in 2024 and close to the 61 percent recorded in March 2022, before Dobbs. The partisan gap is 48 points, with 84 percent of Democrats and Democratic leaners saying legal in all or most cases against 36 percent of Republicans and leaners; among White evangelical Christians, 74 percent say illegal in all or most. This is why abortion polling moves so much with question wording: many respondents are not picking one of the two claims but holding both.
stats.source_label: Pew Research Center, survey of 8,512 US adults, January 20-26, 2026

stats.label: Abortions worldwide each year
stats.note: An estimated 73.3 million abortions occurred each year worldwide between 2015 and 2019, a rate of 39 per 1,000 women aged 15-49; the model’s uncertainty interval runs from 66.7 to 82.0 million.
stats.detail: The same model estimates 121.0 million unintended pregnancies a year, 61 percent of which end in abortion; WHO’s fact sheet of December 2025 puts it another way, that three in ten of all pregnancies end in induced abortion. Between 1990-1994 and 2015-2019 the global unintended pregnancy rate fell from 79 to 64 per 1,000 women while the share of unintended pregnancies ending in abortion rose from 51 to 61 percent, leaving the abortion rate roughly where it was thirty years earlier. The model also finds similar rates under permissive and restrictive law, 40 per 1,000 women where abortion is broadly legal against 36 where it is restricted, and a higher rate in restrictive countries once China and India are set aside; Guttmacher notes the counterpoint inside its own data, that among high-income countries the rate is 11 where abortion is broadly legal and 32 where it is not. These are modeled estimates built from surveys, official statistics and published studies, and they are disputed by those who think abortion under restrictive law is systematically undercounted, and by those who think it is overcounted.
stats.source_label: Bearak et al., The Lancet Global Health 8(9), 2020 (Guttmacher Institute and WHO model)

stats.label: US abortions by 13 weeks of gestation
stats.note: In 2022, 92.8 percent of reported US abortions occurred at or before thirteen weeks of gestation and 1.1 percent at twenty-one weeks or later; an independent count finds a similar shape.
stats.detail: The CDC puts 41.6 percent of 2022 abortions at six weeks or earlier, 37.0 percent at seven to nine weeks, 14.2 percent at ten to thirteen weeks and 6.1 percent at fourteen to twenty weeks, leaving 78.6 percent at or before nine weeks. Almost the whole argument about late abortion concerns the last fraction of a percent, and almost the whole practice concerns the first trimester. Reporting to the CDC is voluntary: the 2022 report covers 613,383 abortions from 48 reporting areas, with California, Maryland and New Hampshire absent, so the count sits well below the roughly 930,000 to 1,030,000 the Guttmacher Institute estimates for the same period from a census of providers. Guttmacher’s distribution is close but not identical, at 40 percent by six weeks, 53 percent at seven to thirteen weeks and 7 percent at fourteen weeks or later. The share at nine weeks or earlier has climbed from 75.0 percent in 2013 as medication abortion displaced procedures.
stats.source_label: CDC, Abortion Surveillance — United States, 2022, MMWR Surveillance Summaries 73(7)

stats.label: Earliest age at which a fetus might feel pain
stats.note: The Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists concludes that fetal pain before 28 weeks is unlikely; Derbyshire and Bockmann argue it cannot be ruled out before 24 weeks, possibly from 12.
stats.detail: The disagreement is less about anatomy, which both sides broadly accept, than about what pain requires. The College’s 2010 working party held that the cortex is necessary and that connections from the periphery to the cortex are not intact before 24 weeks; its 2022 review surveyed the literature since then, took in the International Association for the Study of Pain’s 2020 redefinition of pain as an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience, moved the threshold later rather than earlier, and found no basis for giving the fetus analgesia before a first- or second-trimester termination. Derbyshire and Bockmann, who state in their paper that they disagree with each other about the morality of abortion, argue that recent work questions the necessity of the cortex and shows functional thalamic connections into the subplate well before 24 weeks, and that an experience of pain without self-reflection would still matter morally. Fetal pain statutes in several US states rest on the earlier reading, most obstetric bodies on the later one. Both sides agree that the fetus shows withdrawal and stress responses long before anyone claims it is conscious, and that reflexes are not evidence of experience.
stats.source_label: RCOG, Fetal Awareness Evidence Review, 2022; Derbyshire and Bockmann, Journal of Medical Ethics, 2020

stats.label: Human embryos that do not survive to birth naturally
stats.note: Jarvis estimates that 40 to 60 percent of human embryos conceived naturally by normally fertile women are lost before birth, 10 to 40 percent of them before implantation.
stats.detail: The figure is in the debate because of an argument it is used for: if most fertilizations end in loss without anyone treating it as a mass death, something about locating moral status at fertilization is said to need explaining. Those who hold that view answer that high natural mortality has never been thought to lower the standing of a class of beings, infant mortality having once been near 40 percent, and that failing to prevent a death is not the same as causing one. Jarvis’s own contribution revises the number downward: he argues that widely repeated figures of 70 percent or higher come from studies mixing sub-fertile with fertile women, and puts loss between implantation and clinical recognition at 21 to 32 percent. Twinning supplies a separate argument on the same ground, since a single embryo can divide into two individuals up to around fourteen days after fertilization, which some philosophers take to mean a particular person does not yet exist before then, and others take to mean only that individuation is more complicated than it looks.
stats.source_label: Jarvis, “Estimating limits for natural human embryo mortality,” F1000Research, 2016

stats.label: Americans who say abortion should be legal, by stage
stats.note: Asked separately about each third of pregnancy, 69 percent of Americans said abortion should generally be legal in the first three months, 37 percent in the second and 22 percent in the last.
stats.detail: All three readings were the highest Gallup had recorded since it began the trend in 1996, after rises of seven to eight points the year before, and Gallup has not repeated the trimester battery since, so 2023 remains the latest reading on its topic page. The shape matters more than the levels: support falls by about half between the first and second thirds of pregnancy, and by half again in the last. That gradient is the most robust finding in abortion polling, and it is why framing a question around all circumstances rather than around the first trimester can move the apparent majority by thirty points. In the same poll 59 percent opposed laws banning abortion once fetal cardiac activity can be detected, usually around six weeks. Gallup’s core trend in May 2026 found 33 percent saying abortion should be legal under any circumstances, 15 percent in most, 32 percent in only a few and 17 percent illegal in all circumstances, with 53 percent calling themselves pro-choice and 42 percent pro-life.
stats.source_label: Gallup, “Broader Support for Abortion Rights Continues Post-Dobbs,” 1,011 US adults, May 2023

stats.label: Rise in births in US states that banned abortion
stats.note: States that banned abortion after Dobbs saw births rise 2.3 percent in the first half of 2023 relative to states without bans, which the authors estimate at roughly 32,000 additional annual births.
stats.detail: The study uses a pre-registered synthetic difference-in-differences design on provisional US natality data, and it is the best available estimate of how much a ban changes outcomes rather than stated intentions. Both camps read it as significant for opposite reasons: those who oppose abortion count tens of thousands of children who would otherwise not have been born, while those who favor access note that the effect is far smaller than the fall in in-state abortions, which they read as evidence that most women found another route. The authors report larger effects for Hispanic women, at 4.7 percent, and women aged 20-24, at 3.3 percent, and larger effects where travel is costliest, 4.4 percent in Mississippi and 5.1 percent in Texas. That distance gradient is the finding both camps accept and interpret differently. The published journal version sits behind a paywall; the working paper carries the same estimate.
stats.source_label: Dench, Pineda-Torres and Myers, “The Effects of the Dobbs Decision on Fertility,” IZA DP 16608

stats.label: Survival of infants born at the edge of viability
stats.note: Among infants born in US level 3 and 4 neonatal intensive care units from 2020 to 2022, 24.9 percent of those born at 22 weeks survived to discharge, against 82.0 percent of those born at 25 weeks.
stats.detail: Viability is unusual among moral boundaries in moving with technology and hospital policy rather than with the fetus, which is why the line is argued over as much as the number. The same study shows how much of it is choice: postnatal life support was given to 68.0 percent of infants born at 22 weeks and 99.8 percent of those born at 25 weeks, and the 22-week figure itself rose from 61.6 percent in 2020 to 73.7 percent in 2022. Among 22-week infants who did receive life support, survival was 35.4 percent. Survival without severe complications is far lower at every age, 6.3 percent at 22 weeks against 43.2 percent at 25 weeks, with a median stay of 160 days at 22 weeks. Those who argue against viability as the moral line point out that the same fetus is viable in one hospital and not in another; those who defend it answer that the question it settles is not what the fetus is but when the state can protect it without conscripting a woman’s body.
stats.source_label: Edwards, Ehret, Soll and Horbar, Pediatrics 154(4), 2024 (Vermont Oxford Network, 22,953 infants)

stats.label: US states by what their abortion law permits
stats.note: As of August 2026 thirteen US states ban abortion with narrow exceptions, eleven cut it off between six and twenty-two weeks, seventeen allow it to about viability, and nine set no limit.
stats.detail: This is what returning the question to the states produced. The thirteen ban states are Alabama, Arkansas, Idaho, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Dakota, Oklahoma, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas and West Virginia; Florida, Georgia, Iowa, South Carolina and Wyoming cut off at six weeks, with Nebraska and North Carolina at twelve. The District of Columbia also sets no gestational limit; the counts here are of states only, and KFF’s own heading of 18 viability states lists seventeen. Limits are measured from the last menstrual period, so a six-week limit falls roughly two weeks after a missed period, which is part of why the shortest limits are argued about as bans in practice. Perception tracks the law closely: Pew found in January 2026 that 73 percent of adults in prohibition states said abortion would be difficult to get where they live, against 68 percent in states where it is legal who said it would be easy.
stats.source_label: KFF, Abortion in the U.S. Dashboard

stats.label: Exceptions in US states with abortion bans or early limits
stats.note: All 20 US states that ban abortion or limit it at six to twelve weeks allow it to save the woman’s life; 15 also allow it for her health, 11 after rape or incest and 8 for a fatal fetal anomaly.
stats.detail: The counts cover the 13 total-ban states and the seven with early limits as of April 1, 2026, and they describe the statutes, not how often an exception is used or how a hospital reads it. Most carry conditions. Among the total-ban states only Idaho, Indiana, Mississippi, North Dakota and West Virginia allow abortion after rape, Mississippi’s exception does not cover incest, and the time limits run from six weeks in North Dakota to the first trimester in Idaho, with several states requiring that the assault be reported to police. Whether an exception applies is usually left to the physician’s reasonable medical judgment, which a prosecutor can later contest. One study looks at a ban without an anomaly exception: after Texas’s 2021 six-week ban, infant deaths from congenital anomalies rose 22.9 percent in 2022 while falling 3.1 percent in the rest of the country (Gemmill and colleagues, JAMA Pediatrics, 2024). Those who support the ban note that these infants were born, and that the study’s modeled estimate of excess infant deaths is not statistically significant.
stats.source_label: KFF, Policy Tracker: Exceptions to State Abortion Bans and Early Gestational Limits, April 1, 2026

stats.label: Risk of death, continuing a pregnancy against ending one
stats.note: From 2018 to 2021 US pregnancy-related mortality averaged 32.3 deaths per 100,000 live births and abortion-related mortality 0.464 per 100,000 abortions, a ratio critics say compares unlike groups.
stats.detail: The study combines national death and birth records, the CDC’s Pregnancy Mortality Surveillance System and the Guttmacher Institute’s abortion counts. Its authors give three ratios depending on what is excluded: 69.6 in the primary analysis, 52.9 leaving out deaths with nonspecific pregnancy-related causes, and 44.3 also leaving out COVID-19 deaths, against 14.7 in an earlier study using data from 1998 to 2005. The gap widened because maternal mortality rose, reaching 43.9 per 100,000 in 2021 at the pandemic peak, while abortion mortality stayed near zero. Those who favor access use the comparison to argue that a ban cannot be justified as protecting women’s health; those who oppose abortion answer that the two denominators measure different populations, that abortion deaths are undercounted when complications present later and elsewhere, and that the ledger leaves out the deaths the procedure causes by construction. The figures cover the formal health system and predate the rise in self-managed medication abortion.
stats.source_label: Steenland et al., “Pregnancy- and Abortion-Related Mortality in the US,” JAMA Network Open, 2026

stats.label: Abortions provided in the US health system
stats.note: 1,126,760 abortions were provided inside the formal US health care system in 2025, and the monthly average rose every year from 77,560 in 2022 to 93,900 in 2025.
stats.detail: The 2022 average covers a partial year from April, the month the count began, and the monthly total peaked at 104,000 in January 2025. The headline finding is that after thirteen states banned abortion the national number went up rather than down, as provision shifted to neighboring states, to telehealth, and to clinicians in shield-law states mailing pills across state lines. Counting independently through a provider census, the Guttmacher Institute puts 2025 at 1,126,000 and 2024 at 1,124,000, within a fraction of a percent; both organizations call their totals underestimates, since they exclude pills obtained outside the formal system, abortions under ban exceptions and provision by non-clinicians. For long-run scale, US abortions peaked at about 1.6 million in 1990 and fell to a low of 862,320 in 2017 before rising again. Those who oppose abortion read the post-Dobbs numbers as evidence that bans are being evaded and that law alone cannot do the work; those who support access read them as evidence that demand does not fall when supply is criminalized.
stats.source_label: Society of Family Planning, #WeCount report, April 2022 to December 2025

stats.label: Deaths each year from unsafe abortion
stats.note: About 23,000 women a year die from unsafe abortion, roughly 8 percent of the 286,000 maternal deaths recorded worldwide in 2023.
stats.detail: WHO’s fact sheet of December 2025 classifies 45 percent of all induced abortions worldwide as unsafe and reports that where unsafe procedures are common, death rates exceed 200 per 100,000 abortions, against under 1 per 100,000 for safe ones. Our World in Data reports that in countries with tight restrictions roughly three-quarters of abortions are estimated to be unsafe, against far under a tenth in North America and northern and western Europe, on data from 2010 to 2014. The historical case most often cited is Romania, where abortion was banned from 1966 to 1989 and more than 80 percent of maternal deaths in that period were attributed to unsafe abortion, roughly 10,000 deaths in all. Those who favor restriction answer that the correlation runs partly through poverty and weak health systems rather than through the law itself, and that a count of women’s deaths leaves out of the ledger, by construction, the deaths the procedure itself causes.
stats.source_label: Our World in Data, “The human cost of unsafe abortions,” on WHO maternal mortality estimates

stats.label: Where the world’s women of reproductive age live, by law
stats.note: 34 percent of the world’s women of reproductive age live in the 77 countries where abortion is available on request, and 6 percent in the 21 countries where it is prohibited altogether.
stats.detail: The counts behind the shares are 77 countries on request, covering 662 million women; 12 on broad social or economic grounds, 457 million; 47 to preserve health, 226 million; 44 to save the woman’s life, 416 million; 21 prohibited altogether, 111 million; and 2 where the rule varies by state, the United States and Mexico, another 111 million. Two features complicate any simple reading. Availability on request almost always carries a gestational limit, commonly twelve or fourteen weeks in Europe, so a country can sit in the most permissive legal class and still forbid most second-trimester abortion; and the category describes the statute, not access, which turns on clinics, cost, conscience clauses and travel. The map is maintained by the Center for Reproductive Rights, which litigates for abortion rights, using categories that follow UN and WHO reporting. The Center counts nearly 60 countries liberalizing their abortion laws since the 1994 population conference in Cairo, against four that removed legal grounds: the United States, El Salvador, Nicaragua and Poland.
stats.source_label: Center for Reproductive Rights, The World’s Abortion Laws map

stats.label: Support for legal abortion across countries
stats.note: Across 27 countries and places surveyed by Pew in 2023 and 2024, a median of 66 percent said abortion should be legal in all or most cases, from 95 percent in Sweden to 8 percent in Nigeria.
stats.detail: The spread is the widest of any question on this page, and it does not line up neatly with wealth, religiosity or region on its own. Opinion in Europe is uniformly permissive even where the law is tighter, with Germany, France, Spain, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, Italy and Greece all at 75 percent or above; sub-Saharan Africa and Muslim-majority Southeast Asia are uniformly restrictive, with Kenya at 12 percent and Brazil, in a divided Latin America, at about 30 percent. A median of 30 percent across the 27 publics said abortion should be illegal in all or most cases. The surveys ran from February 2023 to May 2024 and used different modes in different countries, with roughly 27,285 respondents in the main study plus 6,544 in an Asia-Pacific survey and 8,709 in the United States, so the usual translation and mode caveats apply. The European figure is the one most often cited against the claim that opposition to abortion is a religious peculiarity of the American right; the African figure is the one most often cited against the claim that abortion rights are a universal consensus.
stats.source_label: Pew Research Center, surveys of 27 countries and places, February 2023 to May 2024

stats.label: Pregnancies ended after a prenatal Down syndrome diagnosis
stats.note: Across seven US population-based studies, a weighted mean of 67 percent of pregnancies with a confirmed prenatal diagnosis of Down syndrome were terminated, with a range of 61 to 93 percent.
stats.detail: The same review found 85 percent across nine hospital-based studies and 50 percent across eight anomaly-based studies, and its authors caution that the heterogeneity is wide enough that no single figure describes the whole country. Rates vary with maternal age, gestational age and race or ethnicity, and the review found evidence they had been falling. Denmark, where more than nine in ten pregnant women take up first-trimester screening, is often cited at about 95 percent. The figure anchors the disability-rights argument, which cuts across the usual lines: some disability advocates who support abortion rights in general object to selective abortion on the ground that it expresses a judgment that lives like theirs are not worth living, while others hold that the same principle of individual decision that protects abortion protects this decision too. Several US states have passed laws banning abortion sought because of a Down syndrome diagnosis, and several of those laws have been challenged in court.
stats.source_label: Natoli, Ackerman, McDermott and Edwards, Prenatal Diagnosis 32(2), 2012

stats.label: US abortions provided by telehealth
stats.note: Telehealth grew from 5 percent of US abortions in April 2022 to 29 percent in December 2025, by which month nearly 15,000 abortions a month were being provided under shield laws.
stats.detail: Across 2025 as a whole, 28 percent of abortions, over 300,000, were provided by telehealth. Shield laws, enacted by a group of states to protect clinicians who mail abortion pills to patients in states that ban the procedure, began to be used in July 2023 and by late 2025 accounted for most of the abortions occurring inside total-ban states. This is why the practical question has drifted away from the legal one: a pill regimen a clinician in one state can prescribe to a patient in another makes a state border much less decisive than it was fifty years ago. Both halves of that route reached the Supreme Court in 2026. On May 14, 2026 the Supreme Court left in place, while a challenge brought by Louisiana proceeds, the federal rules that allow mifepristone to be prescribed by telehealth and sent by mail, as reported by NPR. At the end of September 2026 Alabama, Arkansas and Louisiana sued Massachusetts, New York and California over their shield laws in an original action in the same court, as announced by the Alabama Attorney General’s office. Medication abortion accounted for 65 percent of clinician-provided abortions in 2023 by the Guttmacher Institute’s count, up from 53 percent in 2020.
stats.source_label: Society of Family Planning, #WeCount report, April 2022 to December 2025

stats.label: Reasons women give for seeking an abortion
stats.note: Asked in open-ended form why they decided to have an abortion, 40 percent of women in a US study cited being financially unprepared, 36 percent timing and 31 percent reasons related to a partner.
stats.detail: The shares come from coding answers to two open questions, not from a checklist, so they run lower than figures produced by prompted surveys and they sum to well over 100 because 64 percent of women gave reasons spanning more than one theme. The remaining themes were health, at 12 percent, covering both the woman’s health and the fetus’s; wanting a better life for the baby than could be provided, 12 percent; not feeling independent or mature enough, 7 percent; the influence of family or friends, 5 percent; and simply not wanting a baby or to place one for adoption, 4 percent. Fetal anomaly and rape do not appear as separate themes because they were rare in this cohort, which was recruited between 2008 and 2010. The distribution is one of the few places where camps that otherwise share nothing find common ground: those who want abortion reduced through material support read the dominance of money, timing and partner circumstances as evidence that most abortions answer a solvable problem, while those who defend access read the same answers as evidence that women are making considered judgments about their whole lives.
stats.source_label: Biggs, Gould and Foster, BMC Women’s Health 13:29, 2013, 954 women

stats.label: Women who called their abortion the right decision
stats.note: In the Turnaway Study, 95 percent of women who obtained an abortion said five years later that it had been the right decision for them; critics dispute whether the cohort is representative.
stats.detail: The study recruited women just above and just below facilities’ gestational limits, which is what lets it compare like with like rather than comparing women who chose abortion with women who chose birth. Its findings are that abortion did not raise the risk of suicidal thoughts, PTSD, depression, anxiety, low self-esteem or substance use; that women denied one had almost four times the odds of a household income below the federal poverty level, roughly three times the odds of being unemployed, were more likely to remain in contact with a violent partner, and had worse physical health; and that their existing children were more than three times as likely to live below the poverty line. A separate analysis of the same cohort found a 78 percent increase in debt thirty days or more past due. It is the most cited empirical work in the debate and the most attacked: critics argue the sample is not representative, that attrition over five years was substantial, and that asking whether a decision was right measures endorsement of a choice already made rather than well-being. ANSIRH, which ran the study, also advocates for abortion access.
stats.source_label: ANSIRH, University of California San Francisco, The Turnaway Study

questions.text: When does a developing human acquire moral status?
questions.why: Everyone agrees that an embryo is a living organism of our species and that a newborn has full standing. The dispute is over what does the moral work in between: being a human organism at all, or holding some capacity such as sentience.
questions.detail:
Biology can describe the continuum in fine detail and still not say which point on it matters, because mattering morally is not a property a microscope finds. The candidate thresholds are well known: fertilization, implantation, the primitive streak, cardiac activity, the first brain activity, sentience, viability, birth, or a gradual accumulation across all of them. Each has been defended, and each runs into the same two tests.

A line drawn early has to explain why a single cell with no experiences, preferences or point of view is owed what a newborn is owed. A line drawn late has to explain why the capacities it names do not also exclude beings almost everyone wants included, since newborns, people under anesthesia and the profoundly cognitively disabled fail several of them at some time. The gradualist answer, that standing grows as the organism does, matches most people’s intuitions, which treat a failed implantation and a stillbirth at thirty weeks very differently, but it has to say what the law should do with a being of partial status. Nothing here turns on a fact anyone expects to discover; the embryology is largely agreed. What is disputed is which facts about a being generate a claim on the rest of us.

questions.text: Does a woman’s right over her own body settle it even if the fetus is a person?
questions.why: A 1971 argument by Judith Jarvis Thomson split two questions that had been run together: what the fetus is, and what may be required of the woman. Granting the fetus full standing, may anyone be compelled to sustain another person with her own organs?
questions.detail:
The question is contested because it would detach the law of abortion from the status question altogether, and both of the strongest positions resist that, for opposite reasons. One side holds that no legal system conscripts a body: nobody is required to give blood, bone marrow or a kidney to save a life, even a child’s, and a corpse cannot be harvested without prior consent, so a right to life cannot amount to a right to use another person. Pregnancy is not a passive state, carries real risk, and ends in a delivery, and a demand that a woman bear it is a demand made of no man.

The other side holds that the comparison fails where it matters. Parents owe their own children positive duties the law enforces, and a mother may not starve an infant on the ground that feeding it uses her body; in the ordinary case the dependent being was brought into existence, by the woman’s own act, in the only place it can survive, and causing someone to need you generates a duty to meet that need. There is also a distinction between withdrawing support and acting directly: through most of pregnancy, abortion ends the fetus rather than merely detaching it. Where a reader lands depends on how much weight those differences carry, not on any further fact about the fetus.

questions.text: Do legal restrictions actually reduce the number of abortions?
questions.why: There is good evidence on both sides because they count different things: abortions performed in a jurisdiction, abortions obtained by its residents, and births. Pills by mail have pushed those three apart, and the data are only a few years old.
questions.detail:
A ban removes clinics from a state, and the number of abortions performed there collapses. What happens next is the question. Residents travel: the Guttmacher Institute counts about 142,000 people crossing a state line for an abortion in 2025, down from 154,000 in 2024 as telehealth took over part of the demand, with provision to residents of total-ban states by telehealth rising from 74,000 to 91,000 over the same year. Those two routes are substitutes, which is why a falling travel count is not evidence that fewer abortions are happening.

Births are the third measurement, and the one that is hardest to explain away, since a birth that would not otherwise have occurred is an outcome rather than a relocation; the increases found after US bans are concentrated among the women furthest from an out-of-state provider and least able to pay for the trip. Historical bans add a complication: the sharpest birth increases on record came in places where the border was closed and no pill existed. Reading the current evidence therefore means deciding how much of the gap between a collapse in local provision and a small rise in births is displacement, how much is prevention, and how much is simply uncounted, since every organization producing these numbers describes its own total as an undercount.

questions.text: Do the exceptions in abortion bans work for women whose pregnancies go wrong?
questions.why: Bans permit treatment when a woman’s life is at risk, but a doctor who misjudges the line risks prison. The dispute is whether women in danger are treated in time, and whether reported deaths and delays are failures of the laws or of how they are applied.
questions.detail:
Those who say the exceptions fail point to the cases. ProPublica reported in 2024 the deaths of Amber Thurman and Candi Miller in Georgia, which the state’s maternal mortality committee had judged preventable, and of Josseli Barnica, Nevaeh Crain and Porsha Ngumezi in Texas after delayed miscarriage care; in 2025 it found sepsis in second-trimester pregnancy loss up more than 50 percent in Texas hospitals after the ban. A doctor facing prison, they argue, waits until the patient is visibly dying, and when Texas women denied care sued in Zurawski v. Texas, the state supreme court rejected their claims in May 2024.

Those who say the exceptions work answer that no ban forbids treating miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy or a threat to the mother’s life, and that the same ruling held the danger need not be imminent. On their reading the deaths were failures of care and of legal advice, which guidance can fix: Texas’s Life of the Mother Act of 2025 spelled out that doctors may act before death is imminent and may treat miscarriage and ectopic pregnancy, and Texas Alliance for Life counted 203 abortions under the medical exception in the 34 months after Dobbs, from state data. In Idaho the fight is over whether federal emergency-care law overrides the ban; the Supreme Court dismissed that case in June 2024 without deciding it.

questions.text: Should viability be the line the law uses?
questions.why: Viability organized US law from 1973 to 2022, and it is the line written into most of the state amendments passed since, including measures on the November 2026 ballot. It is also a line that moves with neonatal medicine, which is what its critics press.
questions.detail:
Its defenders argue that viability marks the point at which the state can protect fetal life without overriding anyone’s body, because after it a pregnancy can be ended by delivery rather than by abortion. On that reading it is the natural compromise: before viability the only way to protect the fetus is to compel the woman, and after it the two interests no longer strictly conflict. It also tracks a real change in the fetus, since late-gestation neurological development is substantially complete, and it has the practical virtues of being familiar, administrable and acceptable to large majorities.

Its critics answer that a standing which depends on the state of intensive care is not a standing at all. Stoll and colleagues recorded 6 percent survival to discharge at twenty-two weeks in a US cohort from 2003 to 2007, reported in Pediatrics in 2010, and survival at that age has since become several times higher, so the same fetus is viable in one decade and not another, in a teaching hospital and not in a rural district. They add that viability is not even a clean proxy for the capacities people care about, since being sustainable in an incubator is not the same as being able to feel. Those who reject it split in turn between people who would set an earlier fixed limit and people who would set none.

questions.text: Should abortion be a crime, and if so, for whom?
questions.why: This is the most active legal question in several countries, and it cuts across the moral one. Many who believe abortion kills a child still oppose prosecuting the woman, and many who want it lawful accept penalties for unqualified providers.
questions.detail:
England and Wales took one side of it in the Crime and Policing Act 2026, whose section 241 provides that no offense is committed by a woman acting in relation to her own pregnancy, at any gestation, after the House of Commons backed the amendment by 379 votes to 137 in June 2025. The framework governing providers was left in place, as it is in most decriminalization proposals. Those who want criminal law aimed at providers argue that any serious legal protection needs an enforcement mechanism, that criminal law expresses a society’s judgment about what may not be done, and that penalties fall more justly on those who perform abortions than on women; they add that removing the woman from the law at any gestation withdraws protection exactly where the fetus is most clearly a patient in its own right.

Those who want no criminal law argue that investigating pregnancy loss is itself the harm: a joint briefing from the British Pregnancy Advisory Service and partner organizations reported that six women appeared in court in England over three years charged with ending their own pregnancy, that more than 100 are believed to have been investigated by police in recent years, several arising from premature labor or stillbirth. The World Health Organization’s 2022 guideline recommends full decriminalization, on the ground that criminal exposure deters clinicians and patients alike.

questions.text: Who should decide abortion law: courts and constitutions, or legislatures and voters?
questions.why: Dobbs returned the question to elected representatives in 2022; France went the other way and wrote abortion into its constitution in 2024. Since then each side has won in a different forum, so the procedural question does as much work as the moral one.
questions.detail:
Those who favor entrenchment argue that fundamental rights exist precisely so a transient majority cannot remove them, that control over one’s own body and life plan is as basic as any right a constitution protects, and that leaving it to ordinary politics means rights change at a state line and can be stripped by a single election. Missouri’s 2026 ballot measure, which seeks to undo by referendum a right the same electorate granted two years earlier, is what they say an unentrenched right looks like.

Those who favor ordinary politics argue that a disagreement this deep, about what a human being is and what we owe each other, is exactly what democracies are supposed to settle through persuasion and voting rather than through judges; that courts reading rights into a text that does not contain them corroded judicial legitimacy and poisoned the appointment process for fifty years; and that a settlement reached by referendum, as in Ireland in 2018, is more durable than one imposed. Both poles contain people who disagree about abortion itself. There are supporters of abortion rights who thought Roe was badly reasoned, and opponents of abortion who want a federal constitutional protection for the unborn rather than a state-by-state patchwork, which is a demand for entrenchment too.

questions.text: Is abortion for fetal disability or fetal sex different in kind from other abortion?
questions.why: It splits coalitions. Some disability-rights advocates who otherwise defend abortion rights object to selective abortion, and some abortion opponents treat bans based on a woman’s reason as a distraction or as unenforceable.
questions.detail:
Those who hold that it is the same right argue that a decision belongs to the pregnant woman whatever her reason, that requiring her to justify herself to the state is the opposite of a right, and that a ban keyed to motive cannot be enforced without interrogating women about theirs. They add that parents facing these decisions are weighing a particular child’s prospects and their own capacity rather than issuing a verdict on anyone’s worth, and that the practical effect of such laws is to deter prenatal testing and leave women less informed.

Those who hold that it is a different wrong press the expressivist objection: a society that systematically ends pregnancies carrying one diagnosis is saying something about lives like that, and disabled people hear it. They point out that sex-selective abortion in parts of Asia has produced measurable population imbalances, and that discrimination by sex is something the law prohibits in nearly every other setting. On this view someone can believe abortion should be broadly available and still believe the state has an interest in refusing to let it work as a filter on who gets to be born. The disagreement is sharpest among people who agree about everything else on this page.

positions.name: Allow abortion before a set point and restrict it after
positions.steelman: Pregnancy is a process, not an event. Leave the decision free in the early weeks, protect the fetus once it is far enough along, and draw the line where a society can actually live with it.
positions.detail:
In the early weeks the embryo has no brain, no sensation and no point of view, and the only way to protect it would be to compel a woman to stay pregnant at real cost to her body and her life. Late in pregnancy the fetus is a sentient being that can survive outside the womb, hospitals treat it as a patient, and almost nobody is comfortable saying it may be ended for any reason at all. A legal system that refuses to acknowledge either of those facts is one most people will not accept. So draw a line: free decision before it, protection with narrow exceptions after. Where the line falls, at twelve weeks, fifteen, twenty-two or viability, is a genuine argument inside this camp, whose members arrive from opposite directions, some coming down from no limits and some up from none permitted. What they share is the structure, and it is the structure nearly every democracy outside the United States has adopted.

Voters choose lines when they are offered them. Nebraska’s Initiative 434, which wrote a first-trimester limit into the state constitution, passed on November 5, 2024 by 509,288 votes to 417,624, while a competing viability-based measure on the same ballot failed. The objection, pressed from both sides, is that a line is arbitrary, since no fetus is transformed by crossing from thirteen weeks to fourteen. Every workable legal boundary has that property. The age of majority marks no transformation in a person either, and nobody concludes that adulthood is arbitrary or that eighteen-year-olds should not vote. Where two weighty interests change in strength along a continuum, the law has to choose a point, and choosing one where the fetal interest has plainly grown and the woman has had a real chance to decide is judgment, not evasion.
positions.proponents: Idahoans United for Women and Families; Lindsey Graham

positions.name: Leave the decision to the pregnant woman
positions.steelman: The question is not when a fetus becomes valuable. It is who decides. The person who carries the risk and lives with the outcome is the person entitled to make the call.
positions.detail:
Pregnancy happens inside one person’s body, carries risks only she bears, and reshapes a life only she will live. A state that can require a woman to remain pregnant can require her to do anything with her body, and it requires it of no one else. The claim is not that abortion is trivial; it is that the person who must live with the decision is the one entitled to make it, with her clinician, on her own moral terms. Laws that intervene do not produce fewer abortions, only later and more dangerous ones, and they turn miscarriage and stillbirth into matters for the police. Many in this camp accept medical regulation of how and by whom abortion is provided. What they reject is the state deciding whether, and a gestational cutoff enforced through criminal law is that decision wearing another hat.

The strongest objection is that this reasoning has no stopping point: if only the woman’s decision counts, it counts at thirty-eight weeks as much as at six. The answer is that the objection imagines a problem the evidence does not show. Canada has had no criminal abortion law since the Supreme Court struck down its provisions in R v Morgentaler in 1988, and abortion there remains concentrated in early pregnancy, because no woman carries a pregnancy for eight months and then ends it casually; the rare very late cases are fatal anomalies or acute danger. Clinical judgment and professional regulation already constrain practice. Replacing them with criminal law does not prevent the hypothetical case. It prosecutes real women who miscarried.
positions.proponents: Center for Reproductive Rights; Tonia Antoniazzi; National Network of Abortion Funds

positions.name: Protect unborn human life from conception
positions.steelman: Either human beings have equal worth because of what they are, or worth depends on what they can currently do — and then the weak are always at the mercy of the strong.
positions.detail:
Embryology is not in dispute. At fertilization a new, distinct, self-directing human organism exists, with its own genome and its own trajectory, needing only time and nourishment, exactly as a newborn does. Every line proposed after that marks a stage in one continuous life, not the arrival of a new being, and the attempts to find a non-arbitrary later one have never converged: implantation, the primitive streak, cardiac activity, brain activity, sentience, viability and birth have all been proposed, and each excludes beings its own proposer wants included elsewhere. Abortion is on this view the largest single cause of human death in the world, and the answer to that cannot be a line drawn where the victims stop being visible. Protecting them is not an imposition of religion; it is the principle all other human rights rest on.

Outside abortion the law already treats the unborn as victims, in fetal homicide statutes in most states, in wrongful-death actions, and in the Alabama Supreme Court’s holding in LePage v. Center for Reproductive Medicine, in February 2024, that frozen embryos are children under that state’s wrongful-death act. The legislature immunized fertility clinics three weeks later, which critics read as the position’s reductio and its members as a political concession, not a philosophical one. Prenatal medicine points the same way, treating the fetus as a patient in its own right. As for the argument that no one may be compelled to sustain another with her own body, the analogy fails where it decides things: the child exists in the only place it can exist because of an act its parents performed, the law everywhere recognizes that bringing a dependent into being creates duties, and abortion ends the fetus directly rather than merely withdrawing support.
positions.proponents: Catholic Church; Robert P. George; Americans United for Life; Secular Pro-Life

positions.name: Settle abortion law through legislatures and voters
positions.steelman: The moral question will not be resolved by argument, so the legitimate way to decide the law is the ordinary one: elections, legislation, referendums, and the freedom to change your mind.
positions.detail:
People disagree in good faith about what a human embryo is and what is owed to it, and no argument on offer is going to convince the other side. When a society cannot agree on a first-order question of that kind, the answer should come from persuasion and votes. In the United States that process was foreclosed for fifty years by a decision whose constitutional basis few could defend without embarrassment, and the result was not peace but a radicalized politics in which every judicial appointment became a proxy war. Returning the question to voters does not answer it, and is not meant to. It means the answer can be revised, that it varies with the people it governs, and that whoever loses lost an argument rather than a lawsuit.

The question has been put to voters since, repeatedly and with real stakes: by mid-2026 twelve states had approved abortion-rights ballot measures and three had rejected them, with four more on the November 3, 2026 ballot. Ireland’s 2018 referendum, which repealed the Eighth Amendment by 66.4 percent to 33.6 percent on a turnout of 64.1 percent after a citizens’ assembly, is the model of a settlement that stuck, while the American settlement imposed in 1973 never acquired that kind of acceptance. The strongest objection is that fundamental rights are exactly what majorities do not get to vote on, and that this camp would not apply its procedural rule to free speech or racial equality. The answer is that a right has to be identified before it can be entrenched, and what is disputed here is whether this one exists at all. The objection also cuts both ways: those who believe an unborn child has a right to life say with equal force that no majority may vote it away, and a procedural rule suspended whenever one side feels certain is not a rule.

positions.name: Reduce abortion by removing the reasons women seek it
positions.steelman: Ask women why they end pregnancies and the answers are about money, timing and support, not philosophy. Change those and the number falls without anyone being punished.
positions.detail:
Both of the loud camps have accepted a false choice, that the only thing worth arguing about is whether abortion is legal. A society that forces the choice and then argues about whether to punish it has failed twice. The work that would actually reduce abortion is the work nobody is doing: paid leave, childcare, housing, health care, child support enforcement, accommodation at school and at work, and contraception for those who want it. The Guttmacher Institute reports that 41 percent of US abortion patients have incomes below the federal poverty level. Abortion is a symptom of a society organized as though pregnancy were a private misfortune; criminalizing it treats the symptom and punishes the person least able to bear the cost, while celebrating it declares the underlying failure acceptable. The measure of success is fewer women in the position of having to choose, not which side wins a court case.

The objection from both sides is that this is an evasion: someone who thinks abortion is killing cannot be satisfied with childcare subsidies, and someone who thinks it is a right cannot accept being told she should not need one. The answer is that this camp is not refusing to take a position but refusing to accept that the position determines the outcome. Its members differ on what the law should say, and several hold that abortion should be legally restricted. What unites them is the claim, supported by the reasons women themselves give, that law is a small lever and material support is a large one, and that a movement spending everything on the small lever has mistaken the argument for the goal.
positions.proponents: Feminists for Life; Democrats for Life of America

crux.lead: At what point does a developing human’s claim to go on living outweigh a woman’s claim over her own body?
crux.subtitle: Almost everyone agrees that a newborn has full standing and that a pregnancy happens inside one person’s body. The split is over when, between those two facts, the first claim becomes strong enough to override the second, and whether anything ever makes it so.
crux.empirical: Evidence narrows it, and more than either side usually concedes. When a nervous system can integrate information, whether a developing human can have experiences and from when, how early an individual is fixed, and what survival outside the womb is possible week by week are all being measured, and the answers have already moved the thresholds written into law. So has the evidence about what restrictive and permissive regimes actually produce.
crux.values: No measurement settles which facts about a being confer moral standing, or what one person may be required to do for another with her own body. Some hold that being a living human organism is enough; others that a further capacity is required. Some hold that causing someone to exist in dependence creates a duty the law may enforce; others that no duty can be enforced against a body.

actions.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, “Abortion”
actions.description: A peer-reviewed survey of the arguments on all sides, from personhood to bodily autonomy to the future-like-ours argument, with the standard objections to each, written for readers without philosophy.

actions.title: KFF, Abortion in the U.S. Dashboard
actions.description: A current map and tables of what every US state’s law permits, which exceptions apply, and how the picture has changed since Dobbs returned the question to the states.

actions.title: Judith Jarvis Thomson, “A Defense of Abortion”
actions.description: The 1971 paper that set out the bodily-autonomy argument, including the violinist thought experiment, and the most discussed article in the philosophical literature on the subject.
actions.for_position: Leave the decision to the pregnant woman

actions.title: Don Marquis, “Why Abortion Is Immoral”
actions.description: The 1989 paper arguing that killing is wrong because it deprives a being of a valuable future, and that this holds for a fetus whether or not it is yet a person. The most cited secular case.
actions.for_position: Protect unborn human life from conception

actions.title: WHO Global Abortion Policies Database
actions.description: A country-by-country database of abortion law and the gestational limit each country sets, the quickest way to see where any proposed line would place a given jurisdiction.
actions.for_position: Allow abortion before a set point and restrict it after

actions.title: KFF, abortion on the 2026 ballot
actions.description: A plain summary of each abortion measure on the November 2026 ballot in Missouri, Idaho, Nevada and Virginia, with what a yes and a no vote would do in each state.
actions.for_position: Settle abortion law through legislatures and voters

actions.title: AbortionFinder
actions.description: A directory of verified abortion providers and telehealth services by US location, with each state’s current legal requirements, waiting periods and age rules.
actions.for_position: Leave the decision to the pregnant woman

actions.title: Option Line, pregnancy help directory
actions.description: A referral line and searchable directory, run by Heartbeat International, connecting pregnant women to local centers offering material support, counseling and services.

actions.description: A network of local funds that pay for abortion care, travel and lodging for people who cannot otherwise afford or reach it; donations can be directed to a specific fund.

primary_image_prompt:
A minimalist flat vector-style icon illustration, in a clean editorial line-art style: A clinic ultrasound cart is the dominant mass, standing right of center with a large rounded monitor whose screen holds only an abstract wedge-shaped scan cone with three plain sweep arcs inside it and no object of any kind within the cone; its handheld probe hangs on a coiled cord that crosses in front of the cart's base. Behind and overlapping the cart's left edge stands a tall wall calendar, its grid of week squares partly hidden by the monitor. Low and small at the front sits a closed statute book with a ribbon marker, overlapping the cart's wheels. A small domed legislative building sits far back on the left at the end of a curving path that sweeps out of the lower left corner, past the book, and behind the cart, over a gently rounded ground mound rather than a flat line. A thin horizon curve runs edge to edge behind everything.

Composition: one dominant focal mass with smaller supporting elements at clearly different scales (big, medium, small); at least one element overlaps another so the scene has depth; the ground is a gentle curve, never a flat line; one connective element runs across the frame to tie the pieces together. A single coherent scene, not a row of separate objects. Centered with generous, even padding.

Style: monoline line art with ONE uniform stroke weight on every element, including the thinnest wisps and lines. Rounded line caps and corners. Confident, slightly bold strokes so it stays legible when small. No fussy internal detail.

Color: a single hue, two tones only. Draw all lines in solid #b8653f, and give every major mass a clearly visible soft fill of the same hue at about 15-18% opacity, so the duotone is obviously present rather than white interiors. No other colors, no gradients, no shadows, no 3D, no texture.

Important: NO border, NO frame, NO box or outline around the scene, just the illustration on a plain white background. No text, letters, or numbers. No human figures or faces. Calm, neutral, editorial mood: show the subject plainly, neither celebrating nor warning. Also avoid: no coat hangers, no protest signs or placards, no slogans or lettering of any kind, no hearts, no halos, no crosses, no praying hands, no fetus or embryo or infant outline anywhere, nothing figurative inside the scan cone, no cradled or held fetus, no clasped adult hands, no people or faces or body parts, no blood, no scales of justice, no gavel, no ribbons or awareness symbols, no arrows, no mirrored or symmetrical two-sided layout, no speech bubbles, no frame or border, no second hue, no shading gradients
